mythologySignificance:
Khandoba is worshipped as a form of Bhairava / Martanda — guardian deity of many Marathi families. Yellow turmeric (bhandara) offerings colour the entire hill.

Classical pilgrimage teaching places Khandoba Temple, Jejuri within India’s tirtha network: a location where devotion to Lord Khandoba (Martanda Bhairava) is believed to ripen vows more readily than in ordinary space. Epic, Puranic, and regional mahatmya literature — not a single uniform text — sustain this sense of sacred geography.
localBeliefs:
In popular pilgrimage memory, Khandoba Temple, Jejuri is especially associated with Turmeric-smeared hill temple of Khandoba. Guides and elders retell this identity to first-time visitors as the living ‘reason’ the tirtha draws crowds.

Local sthala-purana and priestly teaching at Khandoba Temple, Jejuri elaborate how Lord Khandoba (Martanda Bhairava) blesses devotees who arrive with vows, gratitude, or grief. Festival days intensify these beliefs through processions, special alankara, and community feeding where practised.

Pilgrims commonly link practical customs — dress, queue, prasadam, and parikrama — with spiritual fruit. Such customs are living belief: they vary by region and should be followed as posted by the temple trust or endowment board.
